articleTitle: Now They're Cooking
abstract: It's a common saying these days that “it's all about who you know.” For jobs and other exciting opportunities, networking and building relationships is paramount. The IEEE and Women in Engineering strongly support networking among members and, similarly, the aptly-named Women in Engineering program at the University of Delaware (not officially affiliated with the IEEE) is working hard to do so as well.

articleTitle: Making Space for Women
abstract: In 1981, Ellen Ochoa, a Stanford graduate student studying optical information processing, watched as the space shuttle Columbia orbited the Earth 37 times. It was the first manned American flight since the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project six years earlier, and the excitement among Ochoa's predominantly male classmates—many of whom had been in contact with NASA for years in hopes of one day becoming astronauts themselves—was contagious.

articleTitle: Bringing Relief to Pakistan
abstract: When major monsoons hit Pakistan in the summer of 2010, setting off the worst flooding the country has ever seen, Engro Corporation sprung into action. Since August 2010, the company has been working to bring relief to the 15–20 million Pakistanis suffering from health and technology problems caused by the flooding.

articleTitle: Blossoming into Engineering
abstract: Ramalatha Marimuthu had already interviewed for admission to medical school when she told her father she didn't want to be a doctor, and so began what she calls the “war at home.” This was back in the 1980s in Rajapalayam, a rural community at the southernmost tip of India, where she grew up in a compound family close to her grandparents and cousins.

articleTitle: Honoring Three Inspiring Women in Technology
abstract: Dr. Anita Borg had a unique capacity to mix technical expertise and fearless vision that inspired, motivated, and moved women to embrace technology instead of fearing or ignoring it. She touched and changed the lives of countless women in the computing fields and beyond. She is responsible for including women in the technological revolution—not as bystanders, but as active participants and leaders.

articleTitle: The Complexity of Connecting People [Women to Watch]
abstract: Technology is revolutionizing both our personal and professional lives. Advances in technology have revolutionized the way in which people work, communicate, and the way they live-simplifying and streamlining every profession and activity. The tasks of many can now be done by a few or even a single person. Automation is pervasive in our daily lives. Technology has also made collaboration an integral part of our daily lives, enabling virtual communities to instantly share all types of information across the globe in very simple ways. However, this simplification masks another fact visible to those who work in the information technology (IT) field- technology is also becoming increasingly complex. Have you ever considered the complexity of the technology that sits behind your "hi" in an instant message, or the sharing of a smiley face, or a "simple" tweet? With this complexity comes increased risk of failure, of skyrocketing deployment and maintenance cost, and of user dissatisfaction. Managing the risks of ever-more complex implementations of new technology is essential to realizing the benefits of increased productivity, simplification of daily life activities, and improved communication and collaboration.

articleTitle: “Top Secret Rosies” [The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: Before the invention of electronic computers, “computer” was a job description, not a machine. There were a number of areas where large-scale, repetitive calculations were needed, including actuarial tables for the insurance industry and gunnery tables for the military. Despite the tradition of mathematics-based careers being male dominated and the male-oriented nature of the industries using such computers, women were prominent in the field.

articleTitle: Focus: HOPE [Pipelining: Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: For the past 42 years, Focus: HOPE has grown to become a nationally renowned civil and human rights organization working to bridge the racial divide in southeast Michigan through their food program, education and career training programs, and HOPE Village Initiative—an initiative committed to supporting academic achievement of children living in the neighborhoods around the campus.

articleTitle: It's Never Too Late [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Pamela Jones, an employee of the Northrop Grumman Corporation, has more than 20 years of experience in the computer industry. Her professional practice includes applied expertise in both hardware and software products. She is a lead software engineer who delivers Web-based software solutions with a focus on collaborative environments and provides leadership for development teams.

articleTitle: Making the Most of MIT [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Nadia Cheng is currently a Ph.D. student in mechanical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and her research focuses on developing mechanisms and materials for soft robotic applications. She received both a master's degree in mechanical engineering from MIT and a bachelor's degree in aerospace engineering from the University of California, San Diego (UCSD).

articleTitle: Fields of Dreams [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Gloria Reinish was the first woman to graduate from the Columbia University School of Engineering. She received the degrees of B.S. in electrical engineering, M.S. in electrical engineering, and doctor of engineering science in bioengineering, all from Columbia. She worked in research and development at Bell Labs and at Sperry Gyroscope Company, where she received a patent on a radar ranging system. She married a chemical engineer and raised three children (two daughters and a son), all of whom are engineers.

articleTitle: Living the Dream [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Shouleh Nikzad is a principal member of staff and a technical group supervisor and lead for the Advanced Detector Arrays and Nanosciences Group at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). Her research interests include high sensitivity ultraviolet and UV-NIR imaging arrays using silicon and III-nitride materials, low-energy particle detector arrays, photocathodes, quantum dot based devices, and novel detector concepts. In her tenure at JPL, she has initiated, developed, and managed successful detector and device programs including advanced n-channel p-type delta doped CCDs, extension of the CCD response for EUV and low energy particle detection, high-speed delta doped CCD camera, HAD, and human eye-inspired curved focal plane arrays. She has developed UV cameras for novel UV imaging devices and applications and her interests extend into bioapplications, medical imaging, and brain mapping.

articleTitle: Passion Play [Women to Watch]
abstract: “If you have a passion, consider looking at that passion from the viewpoint of engineering,” counsels Maureen Connelly, a biomedical engineer by training and currently a senior manager in supply chain at EMD Millipore. Connelly certainly followed her own advice, relying on her engineering skills to steer her through a career path that has been very diverse.

articleTitle: The Scientists Driving Cancer Care [Women to Watch]
abstract: A large team oversees an individual's cancer care. There are nurses, radiation therapists, oncologists, and dosimetrists, and then there are medical physicists like Sheri Weintraub, chief physicist at a cancer care center in Fall River, Massachusetts.

articleTitle: The Most Inspiring Engineer of the Year [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: Sunita Chauhan, winner of the 2010 IEEE Asia Pacific Women in Engineering (WIE) Most Inspiring Engineer of the Year Award, and associate professor, division of mechatronics and design at the school of mechanical and production engineering at Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore, calls her career “very enriching and satisfying,” especially when it inspires others.

articleTitle: Tech Sales Pays Off [Career Advisor: Experiences from the Real World]
abstract: Janet Flores, executive and global account manager for Rockwell Automation, a worldwide engineering and construction firm headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, is a member of the technical sales team and is currently responsible for projects in the oil and gas industry. Though her focus is in oil and gas, Rockwell is involved in many industries, including entertainment engineering. From controlling a roller coaster racing at 120 mi/h, helping to protect an investment in valuable exotic creatures, or providing secure transportation to ski runs, Flores says Rockwell works with customers to help them fulfill their project requirements, whether it be automation at the industry's largest entertainment theme parks, Broadway shows, or other venues.

articleTitle: Your Personal GPS [Career Advisor: Experiences from the Real World]
abstract: As you prepare to enter the engineering profession, you can take advantage of unexpected opportunities and enjoy an incredible journey by managing your career. This is accomplished by applying engineering tools to develop and use a dynamic career plan.

articleTitle: Domo Arigato, Mr. Roboto [Pipelining: Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: On the surface it is no different from any other sporting event. The students, all in colorful team uniforms, are intently focused on the playing field. The competition is tough, teamwork is critical, and this event is the culmination of months of hard work and preparation. Coaches help the competitors plan and execute their strategies. But upon closer examination, a spectator might be surprised to find the competitors crowded around small robots instead of soccer balls. More likely to be run by the science department than the athletic department, the Robot Challenge is one Women in Engineering (WIE) chapter's latest outreach effort to improve science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education in local schools.

articleTitle: Curiosities, Secrets, and Rewards [The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: When the women of DePauw University in Indiana gathered for a meeting of professors in science, some of them looked a little funny at Dr. Rebecca Upton, a member of the Sociology and Anthropology department. Though perhaps they expected to see only women in the natural sciences, Upton holds the same strong sense of curiosity that leads others to scientific fields, though she has chosen to focus on the social sciences.

articleTitle: Music to Her Ears [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Like many who have come before her, Teresa Nakra was bit by the technology bug. “People who knew me in college can't believe where I've ended up,” she laughs. A trained orchestral conductor, Nakra grew up in New York and planned for a future in classical music, which she loved since she was a child. But after receiving an A.B. in music from Harvard University, Nakra looked at the path that lay ahead of her and was concerned that classical music might not be around in the same way for the length of her career. “I saw that audiences were aging and young people just weren't engaged with classical music,” she recalls. “I wanted to do something that seemed socially vibrant and new.”

articleTitle: How on Earth Can a Teacher's Reward Be in Heaven? [The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: High school subjects such as mathematics, the physical sciences, and the biological sciences are core subjects that students must study in high school to enable them to choose an engineering or science career. Some of the topics in these subjects are quite abstract and sometimes entail deep reasoning.

articleTitle: Guts and Brains [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Ferdinanda Ponci received her Ph.D. degree in electrical engineering from Politecnico di Milano, Italy, in 2002. In 2003 she joined the Department of Electrical Engineering at the University of South Carolina as an assistant professor. In 2008 she was granted tenure and promoted to associate professor. In 2009 she joined the E.ON Energy research Center–Inst itute for Automation of Complex Power Systems at RWTH Aachen University as chief engineer and lecturer, and she has been an apl. professor at the same institution since 2010.

articleTitle: Rapid Communication [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Valencia M. Joyner completed both B.S. and M.Eng. degrees in electrical engineering and computer science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1998 and 1999, respectively. She received the Ph.D. degree in electrical engineering from the University of Cambridge, United Kingdom, in 2003.

articleTitle: She Shoots, She Scores! [Pipelining; Attractive Programs for Women]
abstract: Soccer, the most popular sport in the world, has a clearly defined set of rules, called the “Laws of the Game.” Players on the field, known as the “pitch,” handle and pass the ball, tackle other players, and try to score goals, but they can't use their hands or arms.

articleTitle: Engineering and Medicine [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Pamela Bhatti received her B.S. in bioengineering from the University of California, Berkeley, in 1989, her M.S. in electrical engineering from the University of Washington in 1993, and her Ph.D. in electrical engineering from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in 2006 with an emphasis on microelectro mechanical systems (MEMS). She joined the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, in 2007.

articleTitle: Dynamic and Studious [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Mariana Amorim Fraga was born in Bom Jesus da Lapa, Bahia, Brazil, on 11 May 1980. She received her master's degree in microelectronics and electrical engineering in 2005 at the University of Sao Paulo, Brazil. In 2009, she earned her Ph.D. in aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the Technological Institute of Aeronautics (ITA) in Brazil with a thesis on “Development of SiC Piezoresistive Sensors Aiming Aerospace System Applications.” Currently, she is a researcher at the Plasma and Processes Laboratory of the ITA and at the Institute for Advanced Studies.

articleTitle: Finding Fulfillment Through Service to Others [Women to Watch]
abstract: Anita Salmon, a senior hardware engineer at National Instruments (NI), a global company that provides test, measurement, and embedded systems for engineers and scientists, joined the company after graduating from Rice University in 2000 with a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering. In her time with the company, she has developed products for diverse applications including sound and vibration, machine vision, and automated test. She has also represented NI in standards development activities, chaired a US$540,000 employee charitable giving campaign, and championed NI's recruiting efforts for her alma mater.

articleTitle: Iran to Engineering [WIE from Around the World]
abstract: Growing up, Fatemeh Tingley had to search to find a place to study—with 16 people living in one house, spare room was hard to find. “I remember studying wherever I could find room,” she recalls, “sometimes in front of the TV, in the yard, or in the basement.”

articleTitle: Leading by Example [Women to Watch]
abstract: One day in 2009, Nita Patel strapped herself into a soldier's gear and maneuvered through the woods and hills of an outdoor training course. On this course, Patel, a systems and software section manager at L-3 Warrior Systems, Insight, in Londonderry, New Hampshire, got a first-hand look at how soldiers in the field use the night vision systems she and her team design and build.

articleTitle: Innovating New Products and Technologies [Women to Watch]
abstract: For many engineers, innovative problem solving is the name of the game, and the women at Cambridge Consultants are no different, except for their business model. One of the greatest benefits of consulting work is being able to get involved at different stages along a product's development journey and also the opportunity to work in cross-functional teams in many different industries.

articleTitle: The Stars Are Aligning [Letter from the Editor]
abstract: On 8 July 2011, NASA launched its last space shuttle mission. The flight of the shuttle Atlantis marked the end of NASA's 30-year space shuttle program. NASA's shuttles have flown 135 missions that included 355 people from 16 countries and have flown 537,114,016 mi (864,114,016 km). The successful international collaborations and interdisciplinary innovations that resulted from these missions are truly remarkable. So it should be no surprise that many people were saddened to see the shuttle program discontinued.

articleTitle: A Major Player in Smart Grid Technology [Amperes: Current Affairs from Around the World]
abstract: Laura J. Manz is at the forefront of smart grid technology. An IEEE Senior Member, Laura is now senior vice president, Western Region, of Viridity Energy, a company that uses smart grid technology to provide businesses, institutions, governmental entities, and university campuses with powerful tools to increase energy efficiency and decrease energy costs.

articleTitle: Pulling Back a Layer [Career Advisor: Experiences from the Real World]
abstract: People working in information technology have long used science training, but information technology giant Hewlett-Packard's (HP's) long-time employee Michelle Rand is using it to work with people. Trained in biochemistry, Rand has always been interested in learning about humans—not just the body, but what she calls “pulling back a layer” and looking at how chemicals combine and what it means when you put them into the body. She spent years doing research in immunology and neurobiology and some time with a biotech startup before moving from Massachusetts to California with her husband and deciding that, for lifestyle reasons, she wasn't going to get her Ph.D.

articleTitle: Call It a Comeback [Career Advisor: Experiences from the Real World]
abstract: Several years ago, Jill McPhee left a 25-year career as an engineer in the computer industry for a more flexible job opportunity in finance, a move that allowed her to spend more time with her children. But after a while, McPhee found that she missed being a part of the hightech industry, and she started looking for ways to get back into it.

articleTitle: On-Ramps into Academia [The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: Engineering FACTS]
abstract: Dr. Mihaela van der Schaar spent seven years in industry before deciding that if she wanted unencumbered, groundbreaking research, then a university might be the better place to be. Likewise, Dr. Lisa Julian spent almost three and a half years in industry as a medicinal chemist, designing and synthesizing small molecule therapeutics, before realizing that she too missed the advantages of teaching at a university.

articleTitle: Stand Strong and Proud [Letter from the Editor]
abstract: There are so many paths that can lead us to engineering and science careers, yet every individual's motivation and journey is different. There are still many young women out there that face cultural, political, or family pressures that may discourage their aspirations to pursue technical fields as a career option.
